column2: alkaloid of Piper nigrum and Piper longum
column4: Measured on human proteins in the laboratory (cells or enzymes, not in people): activates the heat and pain receptor TRPV1 (EC50 about 3 micromolar, HEK293 cells, 2010) - the molecular basis of the pungency; inhibits the drug transporter P-glycoprotein ABCB1 (IC50 15 to 74 micromolar for digoxin and cyclosporin transport) and the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A4 (Bhardwaj et al. 2002) - the proposed basis of the claim that pepper raises the uptake of other substances, and of possible drug interactions; inhibits monoamine oxidase B (IC50 0.5 to 1 micromolar, MAO-A about 60 micromolar); modulates the GABA-A receptor alpha1beta2gamma2 (EC50 6 to 52 micromolar). Most values are in the micromolar range; whether such concentrations are reached in the body after eating pepper is not shown by these measurements. Protein sequence similarity between the plant and humans plays no part: the effects come from the small molecule binding to human proteins.

column2: alkaloid of Piper longum (also called piplartine)
column4: Measured in the laboratory only: kills many human cancer cell lines (IC50 mostly 0.3 to 5 micromolar, e.g. leukaemia lines MV4-11 and HL-60, colon HT-29, breast MCF7) and inhibits thioredoxin reductase 1 (IC50 1.8 to 46 micromolar), which raises oxidative stress (ROS) in the cells; in a PubChem screening assay it was active on CYP3A4 (potency about 0.05 micromolar, screening data, not a dedicated study). No clinical trial result is recorded in these sources; the anti-cancer claim rests on cell and animal experiments.

Ivermectin is not a natural product: it is made by hydrogenating avermectin B1 (Chabala et al. 1980), and the avermectins are produced by the soil bacterium Streptomyces avermitilis (an actinomycete), isolated and fermented by Merck and the Kitasato Institute (Burg et al. 1979; Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2015 for Satoshi Omura and William C. Campbell). The LOTUS records of ivermectin B1a in Streptomyces avermitilis (Microb Cell Fact 2017, engineered milbemycin biosynthesis) and in the fungus Sparticola junci (J Nat Prod 2019, sparticolins) do not report natural ivermectin production - judging by their titles ivermectin appears there as a reference or comparison compound.
